scenes.narration: Twenty-eight dollars and ninety-two cents. Then two hundred and sixty-nine dollars and ninety-two cents. That is how much the price of keeping enough power plants ready jumped, in a single auction, on America's largest power grid.
More than nine times higher, by our calculation. And that cost does not stay in the auction room. It flows, month after month, into the electricity bills of millions of homes.
So why is the most ordinary bill in America, the one for the lights, suddenly rising faster than almost everything else?
By the end of this video, you will know the four forces pushing your bill up. The wires, the fuel, the data centers, and the way utilities are allowed to earn a profit.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Start with the price. According to the Energy Information Administration, the average American home paid about about twelve and a half cents per kilowatt hour in twenty fifteen. So far in twenty twenty-six, it is about eighteen cents, based on preliminary data. By our calculation, the price rose about thirty-six percent in the ten years to twenty twenty-five.

And lately it has outrun inflation. In the five years to September twenty twenty-six, the government's price index for electricity rose almost thirty-five percent, by our calculation. Prices in general rose about twenty-three percent. The EIA itself says retail electricity prices have increased faster than the rate of inflation since twenty twenty-two.

For a typical home, that adds up. In twenty twenty-four, the average American household used about eight hundred and sixty-three kilowatt hours a month and paid about one hundred and forty-two dollars a month. In the summer, with air conditioners running, bills climb far higher.

Where you live matters enormously. This year, homes in Hawaii pay more than forty-six cents per kilowatt hour, and California more than thirty-two. In North Dakota, Idaho, Utah and Louisiana, it is around thirteen cents or less. By our calculation, a kilowatt hour in Hawaii costs about three point seven times as much as in North Dakota. And some of the fastest increases this year are in Ohio and Virginia, where residential prices so far are up about thirteen percent on last year, also by our calculation.

Let me draw what is inside one bill. A slice for the power plants that make the electricity. A slice for the high-voltage lines that carry it across the country. A slice for the local wires and poles that bring it to your street. And a slice of profit for the utility. The surprise is which slices are growing.

scenes.narration: Because the fastest-growing part of your bill is not the power itself. It is the wires.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The EIA looked at twenty years of spending by major utilities. From two thousand and three to twenty twenty-three, capital spending on local distribution, the poles, wires and transformers in your neighborhood, rose one hundred and sixty percent, to about fifty-one billion dollars a year. Spending on long-distance transmission nearly tripled, to about twenty-eight billion.

Meanwhile, spending to actually produce electricity fell twenty-four percent over the same period, after adjusting for inflation. Power plants got cheaper to run. Delivering the power got much more expensive.

Why? Much of the grid is old and needs replacing. Storms and wildfires keep knocking it down. In California, regulators estimate that about forty billion dollars of wildfire costs were approved for recovery from customers between twenty nineteen and twenty twenty-four. In twenty twenty-four, wildfire costs made up about twenty-seven percent of what the largest utility there, PG and E, collected.

Let me draw twenty years of spending. Here is the money spent making electricity, slowly shrinking. Here is the money spent on transmission lines, almost tripling. And here is the money spent on local wires, more than doubling. The bill follows the wires.

scenes.narration: But there is a second surprise. The fuel that powers much of the grid actually got cheaper.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In much of America, natural gas sets the price of electricity in the wholesale market most hours of the day. In twenty twenty-two, after Russia invaded Ukraine, the average Henry Hub gas price was six dollars and forty-five cents per million British thermal units. By twenty twenty-four, it had fallen to two dollars and nineteen cents.

By our calculation, that is a drop of about two thirds. And yet over those same two years, the average residential electricity price did not fall. It rose almost ten percent. Most customers pay a price based on the average cost of providing electricity over time, and those costs were dominated by something else.

keyframes.cue: a drop of about two thirds

scenes.narration: Gas prices have risen again since, to three dollars and fifty-two cents in twenty twenty-five. So households now face both pressures at once, the rising cost of the wires, and a fuel that is no longer cheap.

Let me draw the paradox. Here is the gas price, shooting up in twenty twenty-two and then crashing. Here is your electricity price, a line that just keeps climbing, smoothly, whatever gas does. Two lines that should move together, going their separate ways.

scenes.narration: And now a new customer has arrived, hungrier for power than any before it.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Data centers, the giant warehouses of servers behind the internet and artificial intelligence. According to a report released by the Department of Energy, they used about four point four percent of all US electricity in twenty twenty-three, and could use between six point seven and twelve percent by twenty twenty-eight.

For fifteen years, American electricity demand barely grew. Between two thousand and five and twenty nineteen, it rose about zero point one percent a year. Between twenty twenty and twenty twenty-five, it grew about one point seven percent a year. The EIA says data centers are driving that growth.

Nowhere is this clearer than in PJM, the grid operator for a large part of the eastern United States, including Virginia, the world's biggest cluster of data centers. On July second, twenty twenty-six, PJM's demand peaked at one hundred and sixty-two point six gigawatts. Every year PJM holds an auction to pay power plants to be ready for peak demand. The price went from twenty-eight dollars and ninety-two cents per megawatt day to two hundred and sixty-nine dollars and ninety-two cents, and then hit the cap in the next two auctions. The total cost to customers for one year rose to about fourteen point seven billion dollars.

PJM itself said one auction left no doubt that data centers' demand for electricity continues to far outstrip new supply. Its independent market monitor went further. It estimates that over the last four auctions, about twenty-nine billion dollars, around forty-six percent of capacity charges, was the result of data center load.

Let me draw the squeeze. Here is the supply of power plants on the grid, growing slowly. Here is demand, suddenly bending upward as data centers plug in. When the two lines get close, the price of being ready for the peak explodes, and every household on the grid shares the bill.

scenes.narration: Which leaves the last question. When all these costs rise, who decides what you pay, and who profits?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Most American homes buy power from a regulated utility. The utility cannot set its own prices. A state commission does. Texas rules put it simply. The cost of service has two parts, allowable expenses, and a return on invested capital.

And here is the key detail. California regulators explain that utilities earn no markup on fuel. It is passed straight through. But on poles, wires and substations, the rate base, they can earn a profit. Other things being equal, a larger rate base means higher income for the utility.

How big is that profit? In California, the regulator set PG and E's allowed return on equity for twenty twenty-six at nine point nine eight percent. Every new mile of wire, every new substation, adds to the base that the return is earned on. And the customers pay it back, with interest, for decades.

Let me put the whole bill together. Old wires to replace, and new ones to build. Fuel that swings up and down. Data centers bidding for the same power plants. And a business model that rewards building more. Each one is a reason. Together, they explain why the bill keeps climbing.

scenes.narration: So why are America's electricity bills rising? Not because electricity got harder to make. Because the system that delivers it is being rebuilt, the fuel became volatile, and a new generation of machines is competing with your home for the same power. The light switch looks the same as ever. The economics behind it have changed.
